article_title: What does it mean? Students’ procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education
citation: Krange, I., & Ludvigsen, S. (2008). What does it mean? Students' procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 25-51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9030-4
title: Networked 3D insulin-protein CSCL environment with supporting website
description: A CSCL environment for gene technology consisting of computer-based 3D models (a research laboratory and a molecular level of the cells where students pick up amino acids and place them in a chain) plus a website presenting the problems and the codontable. "The 3D model was organised for distributed settings, with the participants connected in a local area network (LAN) and supplied with a telecommunication system that allowed them to communicate orally during the whole session." Students and teacher, each in a separate room, shared the 3D models and website as shared objects and were represented by avatars.
requirements: A local area network connecting all participants
A real-time telecommunication system for oral communication
Basic teacher training using the tools ahead of the educational setting
constraints: The 3D model comes with taxations, including weaknesses concerning the conceptual representations and a storyline that partly steals focus from the disciplinary problem
target_learning_goals: reading DNA sequences with a codontable
relating codons to amino acids
building a model of the insulin-protein
examples: Students sequenced an insulin gene, built an insulin-protein, and performed a DNA analysis across three days within a four-week gene-technology project.
key_sources: Krange, I., & Ludvigsen, S. (2008). What does it mean? Students' procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 25-51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9030-4

citation: Mochizuki, T., Sasaki, H., Wakimoto, T., Kubota, Y., Eagan, B., Hirayama, R., Yamaguchi, Y., Yuki, N., Funaoi, H., Suzuki, H., & Kato, H. (2022). title: 3D manipulable animation as a perspective-taking manipulative for reflective discussion
description: A modified output of the puppetry system: a 3D animation that starts from a bird's-eye view and lets student teachers "take different viewpoints by clicking on the heads of the teacher or each student" during reflective discussion, showing how each puppet turned and moved and each student's LED-based state. The article situates it among "inter-identity technologies" combining a person's perspective with a different first-person identity, and as a bifocal modeling counterpart pairing the physical role-play with its virtual replay. In the study it was the experimental condition's reflection medium, contrasted with third-person video only.
requirements: Requires the tangible puppetry role-play data to generate the recordable, viewpoint-switchable animation
constraints: It merely replayed the role-play and did not allow simulating computational models like other bifocal modeling studies
target_learning_goals: adopting multiple first-person student viewpoints
empathizing with students' positions
improving dialogic lesson design
examples: Experimental-condition groups were encouraged to click on characters' heads to shift to diverse first-person perspectives during the 20-min reflective discussion

article_title: 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review.
citation: Brumpt Eléonore, Bertin Eugénie, Tatu Laurent, Louvrier Aurélien. (2023). 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04744-w
title: 3D-printed anatomical models (3DPAMs) for teaching normal human anatomy
description: 3DPAMs are physical 3D-printed replicas of anatomically normal human structures used as pedagogical tools in anatomy teaching. They are typically designed from medical image data — "In 47 studies (69%), the 3DPAMs were designed from CT scans" — segmented and modelled in software such as Mimics or MeshMixer, and printed mostly by FDM in plastic, most often PLA. Reported advantages include visual and haptic qualities, reproducibility, customizability, manipulability, and integration of functional anatomy.
requirements: An image acquisition modality must be chosen; the review states choosing an appropriate image acquisition modality is key
Segmentation and modelling software plus a compatible printer are needed; professionals such as engineers, radiologists, graphic designers and anatomists were often required
constraints: The main disadvantages were design-related: consistency, lack of detail or transparency, overly bright colours, long printing time, and high cost
More realistic models require more expensive technologies and substantially longer design time
target_learning_goals: normal human anatomy knowledge
spatial understanding of complex anatomical regions
structure recognition
mental rotation ability
examples: Bone was printed in 51 of 68 articles; the cephalic region was the most studied (33 articles); plastic and its derivatives were used in 48 studies
key_sources: Brumpt Eléonore, Bertin Eugénie, Tatu Laurent, Louvrier Aurélien. (2023). 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04744-w

article_title: The Effect of 3D Virtual Learning Environment on Secondary School Third Grade Students' Attitudes toward Mathematics
citation: İrfan Şimşek. (2016). The Effect of 3D Virtual Learning Environment on Secondary School Third Grade Students' Attitudes toward Mathematics. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(3). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Use 3D virtual learning environments to concretize abstract mathematics for students in the concrete operational stage
description: The article argues that abstract subjects such as algebraic expressions are taught when students are still in Piaget's concrete operational stage, and that presenting a cube, "a three dimensional object, on a two dimensional board creates a separate paradox." Materials built in three-dimensional virtual environments "not only concretize the subject but also provide the opportunity to use them in required place and time," at near-zero copying cost, and can be accessed outside school.
requirements: Three-dimensional online virtual learning environments in which multiple users interact through avatars
Materials designed to present abstract subjects concretely to students in the concrete operational stage
constraints: The article notes the low number of existing concrete materials limits each student's access and confines use to the school; the empirical support comes from a single small one-group study
target_learners: Secondary school students in the concrete operational stage (ages 7-11 and transitional grades)
target_learning_goals: Understanding abstract mathematics content such as algebraic expressions and the Cartesian coordinate system
Improved attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The Mathematics Robot in Second Life was used with 28 seventh-grade students, who found the SL activities more interesting and different compared to classroom activities

article_title: Improving Learning Results and Reducing Cognitive Load through 3D Courseware on Color Management and Inspection Instruction
citation: Liang-Yuan Hsiung & Mu-Hui Lai. (2013). Improving Learning Results and Reducing Cognitive Load through 3D Courseware on Color Management and Inspection Instruction. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(3). https://www.tojet.net/
title: 3D courseware for color management and inspection
description: A self-developed 3D (virtual reality) courseware simulating a color management and inspection laboratory, built so students can practice equipment operations anytime and anywhere when physical systems are too costly to share. It models the SpectroEye III light booth, color checkers, monitors, scanners, plotters and EyeOne tester, and was developed with Virtool, 3D Max, Java, Photoshop, Illustrator and Flash. After expert consultation and trial-and-error correction, it could "deliver images closely resembling the original with an easy-to-operate characteristic". It replaced verbal instructions with easy-listening music to avoid added cognitive load.
requirements: Requires computer equipment adequate to avoid lags; the authors suggest an upgraded CPU, increased main memory and an independent graphics card
constraints: Verbal instructions were replaced by music, and the authors advise future researchers to include verbal instructions in their courseware
target_learners: college students learning color management and inspection
target_learning_goals: operating color management and inspection equipment
color calibration and ICC profile procedures
examples: In the 10-week quasi-experiment, the lecture + 3D courseware group (Method B) significantly outperformed the lecture, video, and image groups on the hands-on post-test

article_title: 3D Game-Based Learning System for Improving Learning Achievement in Software Engineering Curriculum
citation: Su, C.-H., & Cheng, C.-H. (2013). 3D game-based learning system for improving learning achievement in software engineering curriculum. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: 3D game-based learning system for the system analysis unit of software engineering curriculum
description: A 3D role-play scenario game, built on the RETAIN model and ARCS, in which the curriculum content of the waterfall-model system analysis unit is mapped into a company-office game story. Players choose among five roles (such as project manager, system analyst, programming staff), take tasks from non-player characters, complete level tasks such as a requirements-analysis maze distinguishing functional and non-functional requirements, and take an evaluation test whose score is shown to the teacher. The system runs on "a cloud-based (Three-Tier) architecture" with evaluation and member databases and five services: Filter Service, Score Service, Evaluation Service, Personal Portfolios Service, and Game Content Service.
requirements: The article states the game should provide challenge, repeated self-learning and attraction to increase learning motivation, and that curriculum content must be mapped into the game.
constraints: The evaluation was conducted with 63 third-year undergraduate students in southern Taiwan studying one specific unit; the authors note the experiment only includes partial university students in southern Taiwan and specific subjects.
target_learning_goals: system analysis processes in the waterfall development model
software engineering curriculum knowledge and skills
examples: In the requirements-analysis maze task, a wrong answer decreases health points by one, the question reappears, and the countdown resets, giving the player a chance to correct the mistake.

citation: Hung, B. P., Vien, T., & Vu, N. N. (2018). Applying Cognitive Linguistics to Teaching English Prepositions: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 327-346. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11323a
title: 3-D image schemas representing trajector-landmark relations for ten English prepositions
description: Image schemas are "a relatively abstract conceptual representation that arises directly from our everyday interaction with and observation of the world around us", deriving from sensory and perceptual experience. This study used mostly 3-D image schemas to represent the semantics of the ten prepositions (except among), depicting trajector-landmark relations, distance, contact, shape, size and orientation, and aimed to describe locations rather than movements.
requirements: Designing an image schema requires attention to the TR-LM relationship, distance, contact, shape, size and orientation (Taylor, 1989)
constraints: The schemas mostly described locations rather than movements, and 2-D schemas were used only where appropriate
target_learning_goals: spatial and metaphorical meanings of English prepositions
examples: Herskovits's image schemas for the preposition in, shown as 2-D and 3-D figures

article_title: The Effect of 3D Printer and Moulage Use on Improving Stoma Care Knowledge and Skills in Nursing Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Avcu Cagla and Yildiz Tülin. (2026). The Effect of 3D Printer and Moulage Use on Improving Stoma Care Knowledge and Skills in Nursing Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.71068
title: High-fidelity stoma care simulation model integrating 3D-printed stoma, moulage, and peer role-play
description: A high-fidelity simulation model for stoma care education combining three components: a 3D-printed stoma for anatomical accuracy, moulage using "makeup and simulated fluids" to depict "peristomal skin irritation and effluent characteristics", and role-play with a volunteer student as standardized patient wearing the model. Students practiced cleaning, measuring the stoma, and applying the appliance on a 'living' peer in ~20-minute sessions, enabling realistic communication and clinical interaction absent in static models.
requirements: 3D printing capability to produce anatomically accurate stoma models
moulage materials and trained personnel to apply them
a volunteer peer to act as standardized patient
constraints: Each simulation session lasted approximately 20 min per student
target_learning_goals: stoma care knowledge
stoma care psychomotor skills
clinical communication
examples: In this RCT, the experimental group performed stoma care on a standardized peer patient equipped with the 3D-printed stoma and moulage, while the control group used a traditional low-fidelity static stoma model

article_title: Development of effective 3D digital models for first-time learners of musculoskeletal anatomy.
citation: Safir AH, Bird MM, Orczykowski ME. (2026). Development of effective 3D digital models for first-time learners of musculoskeletal anatomy. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70220
title: 3D digital models are most effective when used early in anatomical education, with innovative features, high enjoyability, and alongside other learning modalities

Use alongside other effective learning modalities

article_title: Rhinoplasty Education During Residency: Discussion of Current Barriers, Challenges, and Opportunities for Improvement.
citation: Khetpal Sumun, Hall Anne E., Ibrahim Yasmine, Nabili Vishad, Delong Michael R., Roostaeian Jason. (2026). Rhinoplasty Education During Residency: Discussion of Current Barriers, Challenges, and Opportunities for Improvement. Aesthetic Plastic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00266-025-05539-8
title: 3D-printed rhinoplasty training models as low-cost, anatomically accurate educational tools.
description: The review identifies 3D-printed models as the predominant type of surgical simulator among the included studies, with 77.8% of the simulator-focused studies comprising 3D-printed models. These models were used to teach nasal anatomy, osteotomies, septoplasty, and other specific rhinoplasty techniques. The review reports cost data for these models: "four out of five models ranged from $2.15 to $132.60, with Wampkpah et al. being the most expensive at $550" and production times "ranged from 15 minutes to 16 hours, with Zammit et al. requiring the longest at 20 hours per unit." Studies assessing these models reported high face validity, educational benefits, and strong ratings for anatomical accuracy and realism.
requirements: Access to 3D printing facilities and materials for model fabrication.
constraints: Cost and production time vary widely across models, and the review notes sustainability concerns if prices are exorbitant for programs to incur.
target_learning_goals: rhinoplasty technical skills
nasal anatomy knowledge

article_title: A Novel Competency-Based Simulation Model for Thoracoscopic Lung Resection.
citation: Liu Ganwei, Yang Feng, Zhou Zuli, Jiang Guanchao. (2025). A Novel Competency-Based Simulation Model for Thoracoscopic Lung Resection. The Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeon. https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2702-2239
title: High-fidelity 3D-printed lung model for thoracoscopic wedge resection training
description: A simulation model reconstructed from anonymized high-resolution chest CT datasets and manufactured with stereolithography 3D printing, using polymer-based composite materials to mimic lung tissue compliance. Evaluating 3D-printed models of coronary anomalies: a survey among clinicians and researchers at a university hospital in the UK. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025227
title: Patient-specific 3D-printed coronary artery anomaly models produced from cardiac CT data
description: Physical 3D-printed heart models reconstructed from cardiac CT datasets of patients with coronary artery anomalies, printed in-house on a Formlabs Form 2 SLA printer using white resin at 1:1 scale. Segmentation involved "purposefully removing certain structures to reveal the coronary arteries and abnormality more clearly." Models were smoothed, exported as STL files, and printed with scaffolding removed manually. Eight cases covering a spectrum of congenital and acquired coronary anomalies were produced.
requirements: Cardiac CT scans of adequate quality for segmentation
Commercial segmentation software (Mimics Research 19.0)
In-house 3D printer with resin
constraints: Reconstruction and printing averaged 27±1.7 hours, which may not be practical in a clinical setting
Segmentation with removal of certain structures was to some extent operator-dependent
The in-house printer did not support printing with multiple colours
target_learning_goals: understanding coronary artery anatomy and anomalies
visuospatial appreciation of complex anatomical relationships
preoperative planning
examples: Eight cases including normal coronary anatomy, multiple anomalous coronary arteries, coronary fistula, myocardial bridging, tetralogy of Fallot with separate LCX and LAD from aorta, TGA with abnormal circumflex artery, Kawasaki's disease aneurysm, and ALCAPA

article_title: Evaluating 3D-printed models of coronary anomalies: a survey among clinicians and researchers at a university hospital in the UK.

Evaluating 3D-printed models of coronary anomalies: a survey among clinicians and researchers at a university hospital in the UK. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025227
title: Use 3D-printed models to complement CT scans for enhancing understanding of complex coronary anatomy, particularly for users with moderate or no imaging expertise
description: The article concludes that "3D-printed heart models can be feasibly used to recreate coronary artery anatomy and enhance understanding of the abnormality" and that models "could complement CT scans to display anatomy and abnormalities, and in more anatomically complex cases display structural relationships not entirely clear on the scans for users with moderate or no expertise in viewing imaging data." This supports using physical 3D models as a complementary educational and clinical tool alongside conventional imaging.
requirements: Patient-specific CT data of adequate quality
Access to 3D printing facilities or services
constraints: Cost–benefit should be determined before establishing a role alongside conventional imaging alternatives
Further studies looking at other anomalies may be needed to extrapolate results to varying classifications
target_learners: clinicians with moderate or no imaging expertise
target_learning_goals: understanding complex coronary artery anatomy
appreciating spatial relationships of coronary abnormalities
supporting management decisions
examples: Models were used to help researchers who were unable to fully understand the pathology from CT scans but identified it on the models

article_title: Comparative evaluation of video-based on-line course versus serious game for training medical students in cardiopulmonary resuscitation: A randomised trial.
citation: de Sena David P., Fabrício Daniela D., da Silva Vinícius D., Bodanese Luiz Carlos, Franco Alexandre R. (2019). Comparative evaluation of video-based on-line course versus serious game for training medical students in cardiopulmonary resuscitation: A randomised trial. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214722
title: 3D CPR serious game self-learning tool
description: A serious game developed in a 3D learning environment simulating an urban public space in which the player identifies a victim of cardiac arrest and performs CPR manoeuvres. The player must "reach a correct diagnosis of cardiac arrest, and initiate CPR as early as possible", guided by step-by-step instructions; incorrect manoeuvres cause the victim to die and the game to restart. It was designed as a CPR self-learning tool for health professionals and the lay public and was compared against a video-based course in the trial.
requirements: Runs on an Apple iPad 4; designed for solo rescuer scenarios without access to a portable defibrillator
constraints: The specific serious game tested had not been previously validated, which the authors state limits generalisation to settings with different serious games or target populations
target_learning_goals: recognition of cardiac arrest and performance of CPR manoeuvres per 2015 AHA Guidelines
examples: Used as the game-arm intervention in the randomised trial, played for up to 20 min on an iPad

article_title: Do patient-specific instruments (PSI) for UKA allow non-expert surgeons to achieve the same saw cut accuracy as expert surgeons?
citation: Jones Gareth G., Logishetty K., Clarke S., Collins R., Jaere M., Harris S., Cobb J. P. (2018). Do patient-specific instruments (PSI) for UKA allow non-expert surgeons to achieve the same saw cut accuracy as expert surgeons? Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-018-3031-9
title: 3D-printed patient-specific instrumentation (PSI) cutting guide for UKA tibial saw cuts
description: A patient-specific tibial cutting guide for medial UKA, 3D printed in medical grade Nylon (PA 2200) from a CT-based pre-operative plan. The guide "was designed to be used in the same manner as the Oxford Phase III conventional instruments", with a distal portion manufactured to fit the conventional ankle clamp, and delivered the planned cut through a standard minimally invasive incision. In the sawbone study it raised novice trainee accuracy to expert level.
requirements: A pre-operative CT-based 3D plan of the intended tibial cut
Use with a video demonstration or training, since unfamiliar users made large sagittal errors on first use
constraints: Results apply only to the two guide designs tested and cannot be generalised
In vivo soft tissue makes PSI positioning more difficult than in the sawbone model
target_learners: surgical trainees with no prior UKA experience
target_learning_goals: accurate tibial component positioning in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty
examples: The guide was 3D printed on an EOS P110 and used by 34 trainees and 4 experts to perform planned tibial saw cuts in sawbone tibias

article_title: The learning effect of using stereoscopic vision in the early phase of laparoscopic surgical training for novices.
citation: Harada Hitoshi, Kanaji Shingo, Nishi Masayasu, Otake Yoshito, Hasegawa Hiroshi, Yamamoto Masashi, Matsuda Yoshiko, Yamashita Kimihiro, Matsuda Takeru, Oshikiri Taro, Sumi Yasuo, Nakamura Tetsu, Suzuki Satoshi, Sato Yoshinobu, Kakeji Yoshihiro. (2017). The learning effect of using stereoscopic vision in the early phase of laparoscopic surgical training for novices. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-017-5654-2
title: Use 3D stereoscopic monitors for novice laparoscopic training where the environment permits, and monitor novices closely when they first operate under 2D after 3D-only training
description: The article recommends 3D visualization for novices because randomized crossover performance was better under 3D: "laparoscopic surgery using 3D is recommended for novices as far as the environment permits." It pairs this with a caution: when a 3D-trained novice first operates under 2D, teams should expect more frequent technical errors and longer operative times.
requirements: Requires access to a 3D laparoscope and 3D monitor system, as used in the study's training box setup
constraints: The article states it remains unclear whether novices should start training or first surgery using 3D or 2D, and whether training-box data from novices can be extrapolated to actual laparoscopic surgery
target_learners: novices who have never performed laparoscopic surgery, such as medical students and junior residents
target_learning_goals: acquisition of basic laparoscopic psychomotor skills, including speed, economy of motion, and accuracy
examples: 40 novices performed three phantom tasks ten times each, randomized to start on 2D or 3D, then switched to the alternate system on the same day

article_title: Effect of software facilitated teaching on final grades of dental students in a dental morphology course.
citation: Al-Thobity Ahmad M., Farooq Imran, Khan Soban Q. (2017). Effect of software facilitated teaching on final grades of dental students in a dental morphology course. Saudi Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.15537/smj.2017.2.15627
title: 3D Tooth Atlas interactive dental morphology software (eHuman, version 7.0.4)
description: The 3D Tooth Atlas (eHuman, Fermont, CA, USA) version 7.0.4 is an interactive dental education software program the article describes as "designed primarily for dental morphology education". It contains an extensive database of dental anatomy, including supporting bone, for primary and secondary dentitions within 3D models, plus photographs, radiographs, and micro-CT scans viewable in vertical and horizontal cross-sections, with practical quizzes for self-assessment. In the study, intervention-year students were provided with CDs of the program.
requirements: Students need access to the program; in the study, groups 2 and 3 were provided with CDs of the software for the duration of the course, and exposure time was increased during designated lecture times.
constraints: The study could not determine whether students used the software at home for self-learning.
target_learning_goals: dental morphology and tooth anatomy knowledge
self-assessment of correct and incorrect answers
examples: Groups 2 and 3 received the program's CDs during the course year, and parts of conventional lectures were for some students replaced by the software and for others the software was added to lectures.
